problem: Zero-shot ObjectNav methods (VLFM, ApexNav) assume a single floor and static scenes and confirm targets from a single view. The multi-floor method ASCENT relies on a robot-specific RL PointNav policy for stairs and ignores moving pedestrians.
motivation: Real buildings have multiple floors and people, so robots need stair traversal, robust target confirmation and anticipatory pedestrian avoidance. Robot-specific learned controllers need retraining when the hardware changes, and single-view confirmation gives false positives that end episodes early.
key_idea: Combine a geometric height-difference traversability map with a heuristic block-based frontier and stair planner, VLM-based multi-view target verification, and a Kalman-filter pedestrian tracker with trajectory prediction, all without a platform-specific learned controller.
insight: Multi-view verification contributes most in the ablation: removing it drops HM3D SR from 66.5 to 41.5 and MP3D SR from 48.2 to 30.2. Cross-floor navigation matters more on HM3D (SR 66.5 to 57.8) than on MP3D (48.2 to 44.2). Frontier block scoring mainly improves efficiency, with MP3D SPL falling from 21.5 to 13.4 without it. Explicit pedestrian prediction raises HM3D-DYNA SR from ASCENT's 30.9 to 48.8. Baselines in the main table are quoted from their papers with different perception stacks, so the comparison is system-level.
method: Object-Semantic-Traversable Map: 0.1 m grid with a 3D voxel object map (confidence δ from detector score, FOV and distance factors, projected to BEV by argmax), a VLM-similarity semantic heatmap (EMA α=0.9, object and LLM-inferred room-type text), and a height-difference traversable map (Δh < H_agent).

Block-based frontier exploration: DBSCAN clusters frontiers by geodesic distance; block score V = w1·max semantic − w2·distance + semantic reward above a threshold; greedy nearest-neighbor TSP order inside the best block.

Cross-floor stair planner: once all frontiers on the floor are explored, stair candidates are cells labeled 'stairs' (SegFormer + SAM2) with δ ≥ δ_stair and Δh < H_agent. The robot plans through them, spins 360° for VLM reasoning about landings or a new floor, archives the old map and links floors in a topological graph storing stair entry and egress positions.
Multi-view target verification: a per-instance buffer scores views with Q = S_raw·f_area·f_edge; at a candidate the best near and far views go together to Qwen3-VL-Flash to confirm or reject.

Dynamic pedestrian avoidance: detected pedestrian centroids are tracked by a constant-velocity Kalman filter with Hungarian association and extrapolated 3 s ahead at 0.5 s steps. Detections and predicted positions are inflated by 0.5 m on the occupancy grid, then A* plans the path; discrete actions are used in simulation and an MPPI local planner in the real world.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-VL-Flash (frozen, verification), Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B (semantic map), LLM for room inference, RT-DETR / Grounding DINO / OWLv2 detectors, SegFormer + SAM2 for stairs
setting.training_data: none (training-free / zero-shot; pretrained foundation models only)
setting.action_space: Habitat discrete actions (MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN 30°, STOP) via A* waypoints; MPPI continuous velocity on the real robot

results: ZONDA reaches SR 66.5 / SPL 33.0 on HM3D and SR 48.2 / SPL 21.5 on MP3D. This beats ASCENT (65.4 / 33.5 on HM3D, 44.5 / 15.5 on MP3D), except that ASCENT has slightly higher HM3D SPL. On HM3D-DYNA it reaches SR 48.8 against ASCENT's 30.9.
limitations: Real-world evaluation is a single qualitative episode in a single-floor office, with no quantitative results and no real stair traversal.
The dynamic benchmark is simple (one pedestrian moving at constant speed toward the goal), and only ASCENT is compared. Constant-velocity prediction may not handle erratic motion.
Baseline numbers are copied from the original papers with different detectors and VLMs, so the gains are confounded with the perception stack. Inference runs off-board.
